question: What is Cohen's d and what are the conventional labels for small, medium and large effects?
answer: Cohen's d is a measure of effect size in statistics, defined as the difference between two group means divided by the pooled standard deviation [S1]. Conventional labels for Cohen's d are: 0.2 for a small effect, 0.5 for a medium effect, and 0.8 for a large effect [S1].

citations.text:
4. Regression to the Mean and Effect Size
Regression to the mean is the tendency of an extreme observation to be followed by a less
extreme one when the two measurements are not perfectly correlated. A student with an unusually
high first test score will on average score lower on the second test. The name has nothing to do
with fitting a regression model.
Cohen's d measures effect size as the difference between two group means divided by the pooled
standard deviation. Conventional labels are 0.2 for a small effect, 0.5 for a medium effect and 0.8
for a large effect. Unlike a p-value, an effect size does not grow just because the sample is larger.

S9.title: Statistics Lab Report Guide
S9.text:
Lab Report Checklist
Every lab report states the sample size n, the sample mean, the sample standard deviation and a 95% confidence interval. Use alpha = 0.05 unless the lab sheet states otherwise. Always report the exact p-value rather than only writing p < 0.05.
When several hypotheses are tested on the same data, apply a Bonferroni correction: divide alpha by the number of tests m. With 5 tests and alpha = 0.05 each individual test is judged against 0.01.
